evidence.text:
Visible-Light-Induced Regioselective Radical-Polar Crossover 1,4-
Hydrophosphinylation of 1,3-Enynes: Access to Trisubstituted
Allenes Bearing a Phosphine Oxide Group
Published as part of Organic Letters virtual special issue “Radical Reactions for the Construction and
Transformation of Complex Molecules”.
Qingzhi Cao,
§
Miao-Miao Li,
§
Xudong Mao, Quan-Quan Zhou,* and Wei Ding*
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2024, 26, 4678−4683
 Read Online
ACCESS
Metrics & More

ABSTRACT: The radical 1,4-functionalizations of 1,3-enynes
have emerged as a powerful strategy for the synthesis of
multisubstituted allenes. However, the phosphorus-centered
radical-initiated transformations remain largely elusive. Herein,
visible-light photoredox catalytic regioselective radical hydro-
phosphinylation of 1,3-enynes with diaryl phosphine oxides as
phosphinoyl radical precursors has been realized. This protocol
features mild conditions, a wide substrate scope, and good
functional group tolerance, producing a diverse range of phosphinoyl-substituted allenes in moderate to good yields with high
atom economy. Detailed mechanistic experiments revealed a radical-polar crossover process in the reaction.
A
llenes are important structural motifs commonly encoun-
tered in bioactive natural products, pharmaceuticals, and
functional materials but also represent useful building scaffolds
for the synthesis of diverse complex molecules.
1
Consequently,
a great deal of effort has been devoted to developing efficient
methods for the synthesis of allene compounds.
2
In recent
years, the radical 1,4-functionalizations of 1,3-enynes have
emerged as a robust platform for the concise and efficient
synthesis of multisubstituted allenes (Scheme 1a).
3
Mechanis-
tically, the highly reactive radical intermediates, generated from
radical precursors via photocatalysis, transition metal catalysis,
or electrochemistry, can efficiently undergo addition to the
olefin unit of 1,3-enynes to deliver propargyl radical
intermediates, which are capable of undergoing reversible
resonance to form allenyl radicals. The sequential regiose-
lective functionalization of allenyl radicals enables the 1,4-
difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes while producing tetrasub-
stituted allenes (Scheme 1a, left).
4
Alternatively, a mechanis-
tically distinct protocol is the radical 1,4-hydrofunctionaliza-
tion of 1,3-enynes through a radical-polar crossover pathway,
5
in which a single-electron reduction of allenyl radicals forms
allenyl carbanion intermediates, followed by the protonation to
afford trisubstituted allenes (Scheme 1a, right).
6
Compared
with the well-developed 1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes,
the occurrence of radical 1,4-hydrofunctionalization reactions
is extremely rare and limited to alkyl radicals.
6
Therefore, the
development of a novel and efficient strategy for the radical-
mediated hydrofunctionalization of 1,3-enynes, particularly

targeting heteroatom radicals, to access functionalized allenes
remains highly desirable.
On the contrary, organophosphorus compounds play
significant and versatile roles in catalysis, organic synthesis,
medicinal chemistry, and materials sciences.
7
Among them,
allenylphosphine derivatives have garnered much synthetic
interest because of their extensive applications as synthetic
intermediates, ligands, organocatalysts, and biologically active
reagents.
8,9
Traditionally, these scaffolds have been prepared
by the [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement
10
or propargylic
substitution reactions,
11
which often suffer from significant
limitations, including the necessity for highly prefunctionalized
starting materials and unstable and hazardous phosphorus
reagents, low atom economy, and poor functional group
tolerance. Over the past decade, visible-light-induced photo-
redox catalysis has emerged as a promising strategy for
generating reactive phosphorus radicals under mild conditions
through hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) or proton-coupled
electron transfer (PCET).
12
In this context, photocatalytic P-
centered radical-triggered difunctionalization of unsaturated
hydrocarbons has been exploited as a straightforward and
efficient strategy for the rapid assembly of a wide range of
structurally complex phosphorus-containing compounds.
13
Inspired by these precedents, we hypothesized that photo-
catalytic hydrophosphinylation reactions of 1,3-enynes with
phosphinoyl radicals could offer an ideal synthetic strategy for
trisubstituted phosphinoyl-containing alkenes.
14
Very recently,
Zhu and co-workers reported a visible-light-driven nickel-
catalyzed hydrophosphinylation of the alkyne motif of 1,3-
enynes with phosphine oxides to afford various phosphinoyl
1,3-butadienes.
15a
Additionally, Zhang’s group achieved
asymmetric induction in this reaction by employing a chiral
diphosphine ligand (Scheme 1b).
15b
These findings may
indicate that achieving regioselectivity in our proposed
photocatalytic radical hydrophosphinylation strategy poses
significant challenges. Herein, we present a regioselective
hydrophosphinylation of 1,3-enynes with diarylphosphine
oxides under visible-light-induced photoredox catalysis
(Scheme 1c). This reaction provides a straightforward
synthetic approach to diverse phosphinoyl-substituted allenes
in moderate to good yields with high atom economy and a
broad substrate scope.
To test the feasibility of our hypothesis, we chose (3-
methylbut-3-en-1-yn-1-yl)benzene (1a) and diphenylphos-
phine oxide (2a) as model substrates (Table 1). In the
presence of Ru(bpy)
3
Cl
2

2
O (3 mol %) as a photocatalyst
and K
3
PO
4
(2.0 equiv) as a base, the hydrophosphinylation
proceeded smoothly in MeCN under 40 W blue light-emitting
diode (LED) irradiation, affording the desired phosphinoyl
allene product 3aa in 43% isolated yield with excellent
regioselectivity (entry 1). Then, we employed alternative
metal-based photocatalysts and organic dyes for this reaction
(entries 2−4), and Ir(ppy)
2
(dtb-bpy)PF
6
delivered the best
product yield (81%). Next, various inorganic and organic bases
such as K
2
CO
3
, Cs
2
CO
3
, and DBU were screened (entries 5−
7, respectively), but no improvement of the results was
observed. The reaction was remarkably sensitive to the choice
of reaction media, with no product obtained when alternative
solvents such as DMF, DCM, and MeOH were employed
(entries 8−10, respectively). Notably, reducing the loading of
1,3-enyne substrate 1a (1.3 equiv) increased the yield to 85%,
while a lower reaction efficiency was observed with 1 mol %
photocatalyst (entries 11 and 12, respectively). Finally, control
experiments demonstrated that the photocatalyst, base, and
visible-light irradiation were essential for this reaction (entries
13−15, respectively).
With the optimized conditions in hand, we then explored
the scope of 1,3-enynes with diphenylphosphine oxide 2a as
the reaction partner (Scheme 2). A wide variety of 2-methyl-4-
aryl-substituted 1,3-enynes with an electron-donating or
-withdrawing group at different positions of the benzene ring
smoothly participated in this reaction to give the desired
trisubstituted allenes 3aa−3na in moderate to good yields. The
precise structure of product 3aa was further confirmed by X-
ray crystallographic analysis (CCDC 2311675). The substrates
bearing heterocycles such as pyridine and thiophene were
found to be compatible with the present reaction conditions to
produce products 3oa and 3pa in 71% and 64% yields,
respectively. Notably, 2,4-dialkyl-substituted 1,3-enynes also
proved to be suitable substrates for this hydrophosphinylation
reaction. In addition, the methyl group at position 2 of 1,3-
enynes could be replaced with other functionalized alkyl and
phenyl groups and hydrogen, producing the desired allenes
3sa−3va in good yields. Moreover, a series of functional
groups, such as ether (3ca), amide (3ea), esters (3ja and 3ta),
ketone (3la), hydroxyl (3ra), and silyl (3qa and 3sa) groups,
were very well tolerated. In addition to terminal 1,3-enynes,
the cyclic internal substrate was amenable to this trans-
formation, delivering the desired product 3wa in 74% yield
with a high diastereoselectivity (5:1 dr). We also found that 2-
methylbut-1-en-3-yne 1x was an effective substrate for
producing 1,1-disubstituted allene product 3xa in 51% yield.
To demonstrate the potential applicability of this protocol, we
examined more complex substrates for the hydrophosphinyla-
tion reaction. 1,3-Enynes derived from estrone, norethindrone,
and (±)-ibuprofen were well tolerated and afforded the
corresponding allene derivatives smoothly.

Next, the scope of secondary phosphine oxide was
investigated. As shown in Scheme 3, a variety of diary-
lphosphine oxides smoothly participated in this reaction.
Incorporation of either an electron-donating or -accepting
substituent on the benzene ring of diarylphosphine oxides was
compatible with the reaction conditions, providing phosphi-
noyl-substituted allene products 3ab−3ak in moderate to good
yields. It is worth noting that electron-deficient diary-
lphosphine oxides (3ag−3ai) generally gave a reaction
efficiency higher than those seen with electron-rich ones
(3ab−3ae), perhaps because electron-rich secondary phos-
phine oxides exist nearly exclusively in the pentavalent
tautomeric form to prevent the photocatalytic generation of
phosphinoyl radicals.
13a,16
Moreover, polycycle- and hetero-
cycle-substituted diarylphosphine oxides were suitable sub-
strates for producing the corresponding products 3al−3an in
40−77% yields. Note that the reaction of benzylphenylphos-
phine oxide 2o also proceeded smoothly to afford the desired
product 3ao in moderate yield, while dicyclohexylphosphine
oxide 2p, ethyl phenylphosphinate 2q, and diethyl phosphite
2r failed to participate in the hydrophosphinylation reaction
presented here at the current stage.
To further demonstrate the synthetic utility of this protocol,
a gram-scale model reaction (6 mmol) was carried out under
the optimal conditions, and 1.41 g of the desired product 3aa
was obtained in 68% yield (Scheme 4). In addition, the
phosphinoyl-substituted allene products obtained by this
reaction can serve as valuable building blocks for further
transformations. The simultaneous reduction of two double
bonds of allene 3aa with a catalytic amount of Pd/C under a
hydrogen gas atmosphere afforded diphenyl alkyl phosphine
oxide 4 in 77% yield. Treatment of 3aa with N-
iodosuccinimide (NIS) led to iodo-1,3-diene 5 in good yield
through allenylic C−H bond elimination. Furthermore, the
phosphine oxide group in 3aa could be readily reduced by Si−
H reagent and then oxidized in the presence of elemental sulfur
to afford phosphine sulfide 6 in 87% yield.
To gain some insight into the mechanism of this
photocatalytic hydrophosphinylation reaction, a series of
control experiments were conducted. Initially, the radical-
trapping experiments with 2,2,6,6-tetramethyl-1-piperidinooxy

showed an obvious suppression of the desired transformation,
and the adducts of the phosphinoyl radical by TEMPO and
BHT were confirmed by high-resolution mass spectrometry
(HRMS), which indicated that the reaction might proceed
through a phosphorus radical pathway (Scheme 5a). Next, we
also performed several deuterium labeling experiments to
identify the hydrogen donor for this reaction (see Figures S6−
S8). The reaction of 1,3-enyne 1a and deuterated 2a-d (80%
D) produced deuterated product 3aa-d with 29% deuterium
content at the allenyl position. Replacing MeCN with d
3
-
MeCN resulted in deuterated product 3aa-d in 61% yield with
23% D. When 5 equiv of D
2
O was added to the model reaction
mixture, deuterated product 3aa-d was afforded in 79% yield
with 70% D, and the ratio of deuterium in 3aa-d increased
accordingly with the D
2
O loading. These results indicated that
the hydrogen atom at the allenyl position in the product
mainly originated from protons in the reaction system. In
addition, the control experiment with alkyl bromide-tethered
1,3-enyne 1ab as the substrate gave alkynylcyclopropane
product 3aba via intramolecular nucleophile substitution
(Scheme 5b),
17
which provided strong support for an allenyl
carbanion being involved as the key intermediate in this
reaction. Finally, light on/off experiments demonstrated that
continuous light irradiation was essential for the progress of
this protocol (Figure S9).
On the basis of the mechanistic studies presented above and
related literature reports,
3−6,12−14
a radical-polar crossover
mechanism was proposed (Scheme 6). First, we postulated
that excited photocatalyst Ir
III
* would undergo a single-
electron oxidation by the residual oxygen in this reaction
system,
18
to initiate the first catalytic cycle and provide
oxidized photocatalyst Ir
IV
. This strong oxidative photocatalyst
(E
1/2
IV/III
= +1.2 V vs SCE)
18
can oxidize diarylphosphine
oxide 2 (E
ox
= +1.0 V vs SCE for 2a)
13e
to generate
phosphinoyl radical intermediate I via PCET with the
assistance of a base. Then, the regioselective addition of
radical I to 1,3-enyne 1 affords propargyl radical intermediate
II. The subsequent SET from excited photocatalyst Ir
III
* to
propargyl radical II produces propargyl carbanion III, which
can undergo reversible resonance to give trisubstituted allenyl
carbanion IV. Finally, protonation of the allenyl carbanion
delivers the desired phosphinoyl-substituted allene product 3.
In summary, we have developed an efficient radical
hydrophosphinylation of 1,3-enynes with secondary phosphine
oxides via visible-light photoredox catalysis. Under simple
operation and mild conditions, various trisubstituted allenes
bearing a phosphine oxide group were afforded in moderate to
good yields with high atom economy and excellent
regioselectivity. This method can be readily scalable, and the
phosphinoyl-substituted allene products could serve as
valuable building blocks for further transformations. The
results of the deuteration and control experiments suggested
that a radical-polar crossover process should account for allene
generation.
